stem.text:
Which of the following observations can be explained by the Ptolemy’s geocentric model?
	(1)	Mercury is a morning star and an evening star.
	(2)	Venus has a complete cycle of phases.
	(3)	Mars shows retrograde motion.
stem.ocr:
PHY16011101>
<lvl=easy><part=core><type=mc><mark=2><bk=E1><ch=01><content>
Which of the following observations can be explained by the Ptolemy’s geocentric model?
(1) Mercury is a morming star and an evening star.
(2) Venus has a complete cycle of phases.
(3) Mars shows retrograde motion.

A (1) and (2) only
B= (4) and (3) only
C (2) and (3) only
D_ (4), (2) and (3)

answer.worked:
In the Ptolemy’s geocentric model, the centre of the epicycle of Mercury always lies on a straight line joining the Earth and the Sun. This explains why Mercury never move far away from the Sun and can only be seen just before sunrise or just after sunset.
∴ (1) is correct.
In the Ptolemy’s geocentric model, Venus does not go through the complete phase cycle.
∴ (2) is incorrect.
In the Ptolemy’s geocentric model, the retrograde motion of Mars can be explained by the combined effect of epicycle and deferent.
∴ (3) is correct.

	(2)	Venus has a complete cycle of phases.
	(3)	Venus can never be seen at midnight.

answer.worked:

∴ (3) is correct.

stem.text:
→→	How could the Copernican heliocentric model explain the following phenomena?
	(a)	Day and night on the Earth	(2 marks)
	(b)	Venus always appeared near the Sun	(1 mark)
	(c)	Retrograde motion of Mars	(3 marks)

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Day and night on the Earth

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Venus always appeared near the Sun

subparts.label: c
subparts.text: Retrograde motion of Mars

answer.worked:
Solutions
Marks
(a)	A place on the Earth is in daytime when it is on the side facing the Sun.
1A
	The Earth rotates on its own axis. After the Earth rotates half a cycle, this place turns to the side not facing the Sun and enters night time.
1A
(b)	Both the Earth and Venus revolve around the Sun, with Venus’ orbit inside the Earth’s orbit.
1A
(c)	Both the Earth and Mars revolve around the Sun, with Mars’ orbit outside the Earth’s orbit.
1A
	The Earth is moving faster than Mars and sometimes overtakes Mars.
1A
	When this happens, Mars appears to move backwards in the sky as observed from the Earth, resulting in its retrograde motion.
1A

marking.point: A place on the Earth is in daytime when it is on the side facing the Sun.
The Earth rotates on its own axis. After the Earth rotates half a cycle, this place turns to the side not facing the Sun and enters night time.
Both the Earth and Venus revolve around the Sun, with Venus’ orbit inside the Earth’s orbit.
Both the Earth and Mars revolve around the Sun, with Mars’ orbit outside the Earth’s orbit.
The Earth is moving faster than Mars and sometimes overtakes Mars.
When this happens, Mars appears to move backwards in the sky as observed from the Earth, resulting in its retrograde motion.

answer.worked:
Solutions
Marks
(a)	Both the Earth and Venus revolve around the Sun, with Venus’ orbit inside the Earth’s orbit.
1A
	The Earth is moving slower than Venus and is sometimes overtaken by it.
1A
	When this happens, Venus appears to move backwards in the sky as observed from the Earth, resulting in its retrograde motion.
1A
(b)	The Ptolemaic model predicts that Venus will not go through the complete phase cycle.
1A
	However, Venus is actually observed to exhibit a complete cycle of phases.
1A

marking.point: Both the Earth and Venus revolve around the Sun, with Venus’ orbit inside the Earth’s orbit.
The Earth is moving slower than Venus and is sometimes overtaken by it.
When this happens, Venus appears to move backwards in the sky as observed from the Earth, resulting in its retrograde motion.
The Ptolemaic model predicts that Venus will not go through the complete phase cycle.
However, Venus is actually observed to exhibit a complete cycle of phases.
